concept.name: REST Resource Modeling

relationships.description: Connects REST Resource Modeling to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: REST resource modeling organizes an API around stable, addressable nouns (resources) manipulated through standard HTTP verbs, status codes, and concurrency/idempotency headers rather than RPC-style action verbs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Model state transitions and workflows as explicit sub-resources (like `/orders/{id}/cancellations`) with `Idempotency-Key` and `ETag` headers so clients get safe retries, caching, and predictable HTTP semantics.

concept.whyItMatters: APIs that tunnel RPC verbs through `POST /doAction` endpoints lose HTTP's built-in caching, idempotency, partial-failure semantics, and tooling ecosystem. Clean resource modeling makes APIs self-consistent, safely retryable over flaky networks, and resilient to concurrent edits across years of evolution.
whenToUse: Building public, partner, or long-lived internal HTTP APIs where browser/CDN caching, OpenAPI 3.1 tooling, and intuitive URLs matter.
Entities have clear lifecycles, relationships, and state transitions that benefit from standard CRUD + sub-resource modeling.
Clients operate over unreliable mobile or cross-region networks and need safe retries (`Idempotency-Key`) and optimistic concurrency (`ETag` / `If-Match`).
whenNotToUse: Ultra-low-latency internal microservice-to-microservice calls requiring binary framing and bidirectional streaming—prefer gRPC with Protobuf.
Client UIs need arbitrary, deeply nested graph queries across dozens of entities in a single round-trip—GraphQL often fits better.
Purely event-driven, fire-and-forget ingestion pipelines where message brokers (Kafka/PubSub) outperform synchronous HTTP.
keyPoints: Identify core nouns as plural collection URIs (`/v1/orders`, `/v1/orders/{orderId}`) and avoid verbs in paths (`/getOrder`, `/cancelOrder`).
Model complex actions or workflows as resources themselves: e.g., `POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancellations` or `POST /v1/exports` returning `202 Accepted` with a `Location` to `/v1/exports/{jobId}`.
Honor HTTP method semantics strictly: `GET` is safe and idempotent; `PUT`/`DELETE` are idempotent; `POST` is non-idempotent unless paired with an `Idempotency-Key` header.
Use `ETag` + `If-Match` for optimistic concurrency control, returning `412 Precondition Failed` instead of silently overwriting a concurrent update.
Standardize error payloads using RFC 9457 (`application/problem+json` with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`) and cursor pagination (`next_cursor`) for large collections.

examples.title: Idempotent Payment Transfers API
examples.scenario: A mobile banking client submits a bank transfer over spotty 4G and times out before receiving the HTTP response.
examples.outcome: Modeling `POST /v1/transfers` with a client-generated `Idempotency-Key: uuid` and returning `202 Accepted` + `Location: /v1/transfers/{id}` lets the client safely retry without double-charging.

examples.title: Optimistic Concurrency on Inventory Items
examples.scenario: Two warehouse operators edit the same SKU's safety-stock threshold simultaneously via a web dashboard.
examples.outcome: Serving `ETag: "v14"` on `GET /v1/skus/902` and requiring `If-Match: "v14"` on `PATCH` ensures the second writer receives `412 Precondition Failed` instead of silently clobbering the first edit.

tradeOffs.factor: Deeply nested URIs vs. Flat top-level collections
tradeOffs.pro: Nesting (`/orgs/{id}/projects/{id}/tasks`) clearly expresses ownership and parent scoping.
tradeOffs.con: Nesting beyond 2 levels creates brittle, verbose URLs if a child resource is ever accessed or moved independently.

tradeOffs.pro: PATCH (JSON Merge Patch RFC 7396) saves bandwidth and avoids requiring clients to echo every read-only or unknown field.
tradeOffs.con: PATCH has trickier null-vs-omitted semantics and requires careful validation for required invariants.

tradeOffs.pro: Offset (`?page=3&limit=50`) allows jumping directly to arbitrary page numbers.
tradeOffs.con: Offset drifts (duplicates/skips rows) under concurrent inserts and degrades to `O(offset)` scans in SQL; cursor pagination stays `O(1)` via indexed seek.

failureModes.name: Lost Update Race Condition
failureModes.description: Two clients read a resource, modify different fields, and `PUT`/`PATCH` without `If-Match`, silently overwriting each other's changes.
failureModes.mitigation: Return strong `ETag` headers on `GET` and enforce `If-Match` on all state-mutating `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` requests.

failureModes.name: Duplicate Side Effects on Retry
failureModes.description: A client retries a `POST /v1/orders` request after a 504 gateway timeout, creating duplicate orders or charges.
failureModes.mitigation: Require `Idempotency-Key` on non-idempotent `POST` endpoints, storing `(key, request_hash, response)` atomically in the same DB transaction.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Collection Responses
failureModes.description: `GET /v1/events` returns 500,000 rows in one JSON payload, causing gateway OOMs and 30-second timeouts.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce server-side default and max `limit` (e.g., default 50, max 200) and return `next_cursor` links.

failureModes.name: Leaky 500s and Non-Standard Errors
failureModes.description: Returning `200 OK` with `{"error": "..."}` or raw SQL stack traces breaks HTTP client libraries and leaks internals.
failureModes.mitigation: Use exact 4xx/5xx status codes (`400`, `404`, `409`, `422`, `429` with `Retry-After`) and RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` bodies.

commonMistakes: Putting verbs in URLs (`/v1/createUser`, `/v1/orders/123/approve`) instead of nouns (`/v1/users`, `POST /v1/orders/123/approvals`).
Using `GET` for state-changing operations (e.g., `/unsubscribe?token=...`), which link-prefetchers and bots trigger accidentally.
Returning `200 OK` on synchronous creation instead of `201 Created` with a `Location` header.
Exposing sequential auto-incrementing database IDs (`1, 2, 3`) instead of opaque UUIDv7/ULIDs, enabling enumeration attacks.
Breaking clients by renaming JSON fields or removing enum values without versioning or additive deprecation windows.

sections.content:
## The idea

**REST resource modeling** treats an API as a navigable graph of **resources** (nouns) rather than a catalog of remote procedure calls (verbs). Every entity or workflow gets a canonical URI (`/v1/invoices/{invoiceId}`), and clients interact with it using HTTP's uniform interface (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`).

When an operation feels like an action—such as *canceling* an order or *exporting* a report—you **reify the action into a noun**: `POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancellations` or `POST /v1/exports`. That single shift gives the action its own ID, audit trail, status (`pending`, `completed`, `failed`), and polling URI (`Location: /v1/exports/{exportId}`).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider modeling an asynchronous **refund workflow** on an e-commerce API:

1. **Client submits request**: Sends `POST /v1/orders/ord_91f/refunds` with `Idempotency-Key: 8b2e...` and JSON body `{"amount_cents": 4500, "reason": "damaged_item"}`.
2. **Idempotency & validation**: Gateway/handler checks the idempotency store. If `8b2e...` was already processed with the same payload hash, it replays the saved response; if the payload differs, it returns `422 Unprocessable Content`.
3. **Async acceptance**: Because settling with the card network takes 2–5 seconds, the API persists the refund record in `status=pending` and returns `202 Accepted` with `Location: /v1/refunds/ref_77a` and `Retry-After: 2`.
4. **Status polling**: Client polls `GET /v1/refunds/ref_77a` and receives `200 OK` with `ETag: "v2"` once `status=succeeded`.
5. **Safe concurrency**: Any later `PATCH /v1/refunds/ref_77a` (e.g., attaching an internal note) must pass `If-Match: "v2"`.

sections.content:
## Nouns, sub-resources, and async operations

Three modeling rules keep large REST APIs clean as they grow from 5 to 200 endpoints:

- **Shallow nesting (max 2 levels)**: Use `/v1/projects/{id}/issues` for creation/listing scoped to a project, but expose `/v1/issues/{issueId}` at top level for direct reads and updates.
- **Reified workflows**: Turn multi-step or irreversible actions into sub-resource nouns (`/cancellations`, `/deployments`, `/verifications`) so they can carry timestamps, actor IDs, and failure reasons.
- **Long-running operations**: Any mutation exceeding ~1–2 seconds should return `202 Accepted` with a `Location: /v1/operations/{opId}` rather than holding an HTTP connection open until gateway timeout.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / HTTP method and status code contract
sections.content:
## HTTP method and status code contract

| Operation | HTTP Method | Request Headers | Success Status | Conflict / Retry Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fetch resource** | `GET` | `If-None-Match: "v4"` | `200 OK` / `304 Not Modified` | `404 Not Found` |
| **Create / Action** | `POST` | `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` | `201 Created` (`Location`) / `202 Accepted` | `409 Conflict` / `422 Unprocessable` |
| **Full replace** | `PUT` | `If-Match: "v4"` | `200 OK` / `204 No Content` | `412 Precondition Failed` |
| **Partial update** | `PATCH` | `If-Match: "v4"` | `200 OK` (with new `ETag`) | `412 Precondition Failed` |
| **Remove resource** | `DELETE` | `If-Match: "v4"` (optional) | `204 No Content` | `404 Not Found` / `409 Conflict` |

## Failure modes and API drift

REST APIs degrade in production through three predictable failure modes:

- **Idempotency key mismatch**: A client reuses the same `Idempotency-Key` with a *different* request body. Always hash the canonical payload and reject mismatches with `422`.
- **N+1 chatty endpoints**: Over-normalized resources force mobile clients to make 20 sequential `GET` calls to render one screen. Solve this with selective field expansion (`?include=customer`) or compound view resources, not by abandoning REST.
- **Silent breaking changes**: Changing a field type or making an optional field required without bumping `/v2/` or adding a deprecation header (`Sunset`).

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Pagination, rate limiting, and RFC 9457 errors
sections.content:
## Pagination, rate limiting, and RFC 9457 errors

Standardize cross-cutting envelopes across every endpoint: use **keyset/cursor pagination** (`?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6...`) returning `{"data": [...], "next_cursor": "..."}`, emit `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers, and return **RFC 9457 Problem Details** (`application/problem+json`) with machine-readable `type` URIs and `trace_id` extensions so clients can handle errors programmatically.

## Practical checklist

- **Audit every URI for verbs**: Replace action verbs with plural nouns or reified workflow sub-resources.
- **Enforce `Idempotency-Key` on `POST`**: Store idempotency records atomically with the domain write (24-hour TTL minimum).
- **Return `ETag` and honor `If-Match`**: Protect all mutable resources against lost-update race conditions.
- **Default to cursor pagination**: Cap `limit` (e.g., max 200) and never return unbounded arrays.
- **Contract-test with OpenAPI 3.1**: Run automated spectral/breaking-change checks in CI on every API PR.

interviewProblems.title: REST Resource Modeling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on REST Resource Modeling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: REST resource modeling organizes an API around stable, addressable nouns (resources) manipulated through standard HTTP verbs, status codes, and concurrency/idempotency headers rather than RPC-style action verbs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Resource Handler applies the primary invariant and coordinates with State & Idempotency DB.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, State & Idempotency DB experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Return strong `ETag` headers on `GET` and enforce `If-Match` on all state-mutating `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` requests.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Model state transitions and workflows as explicit sub-resources (like `/orders/{id}/cancellations`) with `Idempotency-Key` and `ETag` headers so clients get safe retries, caching, and predictable HTTP semantics.
Avoid trap: Putting verbs in URLs (`/v1/createUser`, `/v1/orders/123/approve`) instead of nouns (`/v1/users`, `POST /v1/orders/123/approvals`).
Avoid trap: Using `GET` for state-changing operations (e.g., `/unsubscribe?token=...`), which link-prefetchers and bots trigger accidentally.
When to reach for it: Building public, partner, or long-lived internal HTTP APIs where browser/CDN caching, OpenAPI 3.1 tooling, and intuitive URLs matter.
When to reach for it: Entities have clear lifecycles, relationships, and state transitions that benefit from standard CRUD + sub-resource modeling.

putItTogether.title: Putting Rest Resource Modeling Together
putItTogether.summary: Model state transitions and workflows as explicit sub-resources (like `/orders/{id}/cancellations`) with `Idempotency-Key` and `ETag` headers so clients get safe retries, caching, and predictable HTTP semantics.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Rest Resource Modeling before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Modeling `POST /v1/transfers` with a client-generated `Idempotency-Key: uuid` and returning `202 Accepted` + `Location: /v1/transfers/{id}` lets the client safely retry without double-charging.
